problem: RL agents for language-grounded navigation (Gated-Attention in ViZDoom) only handle simple instructions like 'go to the red torch' because reward design for complex instructions needs costly manual, environment-specific labeling.
motivation: Reward (knowing when an instruction is fulfilled) is the main supervision bottleneck for language-conditioned RL. Natural-language navigation instructions describe abstract scene structure, so scene graphs paired with instructions can give environment-agnostic rewards reusable across simulators.
key_idea: Adapt CLEVR scene graphs and functional-program templates to generate relational navigation instructions with known target objects, map the scenes into VizDoom to derive rewards, and train a Gated-Attention A3C agent with curriculum learning.
insight: Training on complex (spatial-relation) instructions from scratch fails completely, while a curriculum from simple to complex instructions and 3 to 5 objects learns (complex acc 0.08 -> 0.30 -> 0.79 -> 0.86), suggesting object/attribute grounding must be learned before spatial relations. Error analysis shows navigation and identification errors occur about equally often; agents confuse the reference object with the target and lose the initial frame of reference. Self-attention instruction encoder was worse than GRU, and a denser reward sped convergence but reduced accuracy.
method: Data generation: adapt CLEVR functional-program and text templates, dropping the query and keeping filters that uniquely identify an object, producing 'Go to [object] [relation] [object]' instructions with scene ID and target identity.

Environment mapping: map CLEVR scenes to VizDoom with 48 object types (8 colors, 3 shapes as column/skull/torch, 3 sizes incl. object) and 4 spatial relations (9216 unique instructions). Coordinates are linearly rescaled and the agent is oriented to match the CLEVR camera so left/right is meaningful.
Architecture: Gated-Attention of Chaplot et al. (CNN image encoder, GRU 256 instruction encoder, sigmoid-gated multiplicative fusion) feeding an LSTM-256 A3C policy/value head.
Reward: +1 for correct target, -0.2 for wrong object, 0 on timeout (T=30); alternative dense reward tested (-0.1 per step, +10 correct, -5 wrong).
Curriculum learning: staged training from 3 objects with simple instructions only, then increasing proportion of complex instructions (0.1, 0.5, 0.75), then 5 objects with 0.5 complex.
Training data: 14000 CLEVR scenes with 5 simple and 5 complex instructions each.

setting.backbone: Gated-Attention CNN + GRU + LSTM A3C (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: 14000 CLEVR scenes x (5 complex + 5 simple) generated instructions, mapped to VizDoom; RL online
setting.action_space: discrete: turn left, turn right, move forward (3 policy outputs)
setting.privileged: none at test time (scene graph used only to generate the environment and reward during training)

numbers.extra: curriculum learning; 5 objects; timeout T=30; accuracy metric

numbers_note: Split is not formally specified (evaluated on 300 instructions); many results appear only in figures. Accuracies converted from 0-1 to percent.
results: Training on complex instructions alone fails, but curriculum learning reaches 0.95 simple / 0.86 complex accuracy with 5 objects, close to the original Gated-Attention baseline (complex still ~0.1 behind). Accuracy was still rising when training stopped.
limitations: Only the single 'Go to X relation Y' instruction template was trained; the other templates are not evaluated
Evaluated on only 300 instructions in a simple synthetic VizDoom setting, with no comparison to other methods; most results are shown in figures
Agent loses the initial frame of reference, and struggles with circuitous paths and confusing reference with target
